passage:
"Anjali, did you see Bruno's gate was open?" Joseph ran up the stairs, out of breath.
"Yes. When I came back from tuition."
"And you didn't shut it?"
"I didn't open it! Mrs. Dsouza's cousin did. I just walked past."
"Bruno ran out on the main road. The watchman caught him near the bus stop."
Anjali twisted the strap of her bag. "But that's not my fault. If I had opened it, then it would be."
"You saw it, though."
"Seeing isn't doing." She stared at her shoes. "Is he okay?"
"His leg is scraped. Mrs. Dsouza was crying."
Anjali was quiet for a moment. "I thought someone else would shut it."
"I think that too, sometimes," Joseph said. "Come on. Let's go and tell her we're sorry."

qa.q: Where did Bruno run after getting out?
qa.a: Bruno ran out on the main road, and the watchman caught him near the bus stop.

qa.q: Why does Anjali feel it isn't her fault even though she saw the open gate?
qa.a: To her, opening the gate would be a real wrong, but walking past feels like doing nothing, so the guilt seems smaller. Twisting her bag strap and staring at her shoes show part of her feels bad anyway.

qa.q: What could Anjali try the next time she notices something like an open gate?
qa.a: Shut it or tell an adult right away, and remember that walking past a problem can hurt someone as much as causing it.

qa.q: What is it like for Mrs. Dsouza when she finds out Bruno was hurt?
qa.a: She is upset enough to cry 😢; for her, Bruno's scraped leg hurts just the same whether someone opened the gate or only left it open.

grounding: It shows a child feeling blameless for leaving a gate open that she only saw, while the harm to the dog happened all the same.

passage:
My name is Madhuri, and I still think about Gurpreet's volcano. Last week Gurpreet brought a volcano model to class. He had worked on it for a whole week, with cotton smoke and red paint lava. He left it on the edge of the bench near the window. At lunch the wind blew the curtain against it, and I saw it wobble. I thought, someone will move it. I didn't touch it. I went to get my tiffin.
When I came back, the volcano was on the floor, cracked in half. Gurpreet's face went red. Everyone asked who broke it, and I said, "Not me," and that was true. I didn't push it.
But at night I kept seeing that curtain flapping. I only had to slide the model back a little.

qa.q: What made Gurpreet's volcano wobble?
qa.a: The wind blew the curtain against it while it sat on the edge of the bench near the window.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri feel it was fair to say "Not me"?
qa.a: Madhuri hadn't pushed the model, so not moving it felt like doing nothing wrong, as if the wind was to blame. Seeing the curtain again at night shows the guilt was there anyway.

qa.q: What small step could Madhuri take now?
qa.a: Madhuri could tell Gurpreet what happened, say sorry and offer to help fix the volcano; next time, sliding something back takes a second and prevents the damage.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet feel on learning that someone saw the model wobble and walked away?
qa.a: He might feel hurt and let down, because a week of his work broke when one small move could have saved it.

grounding: It shows a child who let a classmate's model fall feeling less guilty than if Madhuri had pushed it, though the harm was the same.

passage:
Class 5B note, Thursday
During recess it started to rain. Kashish was sitting under the shed and could see Sachin's library book lying open on the garden bench. She watched it for a while and did not bring it in. By the bell it was soaked and the pages had stuck together.
When I asked, Kashish said, "I didn't leave it there, Ma'am. I just didn't pick it up." She looked honestly puzzled that it could have anything to do with her.
I asked her one question: if she had carried the book out into the rain herself, how would she feel? She went quiet, then said, "Bad. But it's the same book, na?"
Next step: she and Sachin will dry the pages together and explain to the librarian tomorrow. I will keep an eye on how she handles it.

qa.q: Whose book got soaked in the rain?
qa.a: Sachin's library book got soaked while it was lying open on the garden bench.

qa.q: What does Kashish's puzzled look suggest she believed?
qa.a: It suggests she truly thought the ruined book wasn't really her doing, because she hadn't put it there; not acting felt innocent to her.

qa.q: How did the teacher help Kashish see it differently?
qa.a: The teacher asked her to imagine carrying the book into the rain herself, so she could notice the harm was the same, and then set up a way for her to help repair it.

qa.q: What is it like for Sachin to find the book stuck together?
qa.a: Sachin has to face the librarian over a ruined book, and may wonder why nobody sitting nearby brought it in.

grounding: It shows a child who let a book get ruined feeling less guilty than if she had caused it, seen through a teacher's note.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today was sports day. Last week Miss Pinto pinned the race list on the board, and I saw that Yusuf's name wasn't there. He runs faster than anyone in our class. I thought, someone will tell her. It's not my job. I didn't write the list.
This morning Yusuf came in his white shoes and read the list three times. Then he sat on the steps and watched the whole race with his chin on his knees.
If I had rubbed his name off, I would be a really bad person. But I didn't do anything, so it's not my fault. Right?
Then why does my tummy feel funny every time I think about those steps?
Reena

qa.q: What did Reena notice about the race list last week?
qa.a: That Yusuf's name wasn't there.

qa.q: How does Reena seem to feel about staying quiet, and what shows it?
qa.a: Reena seems uneasy and a little guilty, telling the diary it's not Reena's fault but admitting to a funny feeling in the tummy when remembering Yusuf on the steps.

qa.q: When could Reena have acted, and what could Reena do now?
qa.a: When the list first went up, Reena could have told Miss Pinto; now Reena could tell Miss Pinto what happened so it doesn't happen again.

qa.q: What was sports day like for Yusuf?
qa.a: He came ready in his white shoes and then found he couldn't race, so he probably felt confused, left out and sad watching from the steps.

grounding: A child who noticed a classmate left off a race list feels less guilty for saying nothing than for causing it, though the harm is the same.

passage: In the small town of Kottarakkara, the boys played cricket every evening beside Mariamma's shop. On Tuesday a big hit from Sibi cracked the shop's glass jar of sweets, and Sibi ran. Only Thomas saw it. When Mariamma came out shouting, she found Chinmay standing nearest, bat in hand. "You again!" Chinmay said it wasn't him. Nobody backed him up. His father had to pay for the jar, and Chinmay was kept home from cricket for a week. Thomas told himself, I didn't break it. I didn't lie. I only kept quiet, and that's different. But every evening he looked at the empty spot where Chinmay usually stood at slip, and he bowled badly.

qa.q: Who actually cracked the glass jar of sweets?
qa.a: A big hit from Sibi cracked the jar, and Sibi ran.

qa.q: Why does Thomas feel keeping quiet is different from what Sibi did?
qa.a: He didn't break the jar or tell a lie, so doing nothing feels less guilty to him than causing the harm, even though Chinmay was punished either way.

qa.q: What choice could Thomas still make to put things right?
qa.a: He could tell Mariamma, or an adult he trusts, who really hit the ball, so Chinmay is cleared even if it comes late.

qa.q: What might the week at home have been like for Chinmay?
qa.a: He would likely feel it was unfair and lonely, punished for something he didn't do while nobody stood up for him.

grounding: A boy who saw who broke a jar stays silent while a friend is blamed, telling himself that not speaking is less wrong than doing the harm.

passage:
Monday. After art class, Arnab noticed the door of the class hamster's cage was open a crack. It wasn't his turn to feed Pepper. It was Ankita's. He walked past.
Tuesday. Pepper was gone. The whole class searched under desks and cupboards. Ankita cried because she thought she'd left it open. Arnab kept quiet. He hadn't opened it, so it wasn't really his fault. Was it?
Friday. Pepper turned up in the art room, fat and fine, in a box of crayons. At home, Arnab told his mother about the open door. "If you had opened the cage, would you feel bad?" she asked. "Very." "And if you saw it open and walked away?" Arnab was quiet a long time. "Also bad," he said. "Just quieter."

qa.q: Where did Pepper turn up?
qa.a: Pepper turned up in the art room, in a box of crayons.

qa.q: Why did Arnab feel it 'wasn't really his fault'?
qa.a: Arnab felt uneasy but less guilty, because walking past seemed different from opening the door himself, even though the hamster escaped either way.

qa.q: What could Arnab do the next time he notices something like an open cage?
qa.a: Close it or tell the teacher right away, even if it isn't his job, because noticing and walking away still lets the harm happen.

qa.q: How did Ankita experience Tuesday?
qa.a: Ankita cried, blaming herself for leaving the door open, without knowing Arnab had seen it.

grounding: Shows a child feeling less guilty for letting a hamster escape by walking past than he would for opening the cage himself.

passage: Jomon, you say it's not your fault because you only watched? Sit with your Sabina ammachi. When I was ten, in Alappuzha, my brother and his friends broke Mrs Varghese's window with a cricket ball. The next morning she stormed over and blamed Babu, the milkman's son, who hadn't even been there. I was standing right at the gate. I knew. I said nothing. I told myself: I didn't break it, I didn't lie, my hands are clean. Babu's father made him work extra rounds for a month to pay for the glass. Every morning I watched Babu deliver milk with his head down. One Sunday my grandmother asked why I'd gone so quiet. I told her. She said, "Silence was your choice, molé. It had a cost too." That afternoon I went to Mrs Varghese.

qa.q: Who did Mrs Varghese blame for the broken window?
qa.a: She blamed Babu, the milkman's son.

qa.q: Why did young Sabina feel her hands were clean?
qa.a: Sabina felt less guilty because she hadn't broken the window or told a lie, so staying silent felt innocent even though Babu was being punished.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Ammachi's story?
qa.a: Her grandmother telling her that silence was a choice with a cost, after which she went to Mrs Varghese that afternoon.

qa.q: What was that month like for Babu?
qa.a: Babu was punished for something he didn't do, working extra rounds and delivering milk with his head down, likely feeling ashamed and wronged.

grounding: Shows a child feeling blameless for staying silent while another boy is punished, though her silence let the harm happen.

passage: It was pouring, the school bus was already honking, and everyone was pushing up the steps. Indu, eleven, saw Sabina's library book slide out of her open bag and land in the muddy gutter. Sabina, a small girl from Class 3, didn't notice. Indu opened her mouth, then the conductor shouted, "Jaldi!" and she climbed on. She hadn't dropped it. She hadn't pushed anyone. It wasn't her book. The next day she saw Sabina outside the library, crying, while the librarian held up the ruined book. Indu's stomach twisted. If she had knocked it into the gutter herself, she'd have said sorry at once. Somehow walking past had felt different. But Sabina was crying just the same. Indu walked into the library and told the librarian what had happened.

qa.q: Where did Sabina's library book land?
qa.a: It landed in the muddy gutter.

qa.q: Why did walking past feel different to Indu from knocking the book in herself?
qa.a: Indu felt less guilty because she hadn't caused the fall, but her twisting stomach shows she still felt responsible once she saw Sabina crying.

qa.q: What did Indu do in the end, and what could she do next time?
qa.a: She told the librarian what had happened; next time she could shout to Sabina or grab the book, even in a rush.

qa.q: How was the next day for Sabina?
qa.a: Sabina was crying outside the library, probably scared of being blamed for a ruined book she hadn't seen fall.

grounding: Shows a child who lets a small harm happen in a rush feeling less guilty than if she had caused it, until she sees the result.

passage:
Imran and his friend Bhupen were playing cricket in the colony lane when the ball smashed a flowerpot on Mrs Rao's balcony. Bhupen had hit it. Imran was bowling.

Later, Mrs Rao asked Imran if he knew who did it. Imran looked at his shoes and said, "I didn't see."

At home he told his mother, "I didn't break it. I didn't even lie properly. I just didn't say."

"And if you had broken it and kept quiet?" she asked.

Imran thought. "That would be really bad."

"So what's different now?"

Imran scratched his knee. Mrs Rao was still sweeping up soil, and the pot was still broken. "Not much," he admitted quietly.

qa.q: What did Imran tell Mrs Rao when she asked who broke the pot?
qa.a: He looked at his shoes and said, "I didn't see."

qa.q: Why did Imran feel his silence was not as bad as breaking the pot?
qa.a: He felt less guilty because he hadn't hit the ball himself, so keeping quiet seemed innocent to him.

qa.q: What could Imran do now to make things right?
qa.a: He could go with Bhupen to Mrs Rao, tell her what happened and offer to help clean up or replace the pot.

qa.q: How might Mrs Rao feel after Imran said he didn't see?
qa.a: She may feel let down or suspicious, since she was left sweeping up with no answer.

grounding: A child feels less guilty for staying silent about harm than for causing it, until he sees the harm is the same.

passage:
"Farhan, did you see Kunal's cycle?"

"The tyre's flat, Ammi."

"It was fine this morning. Did someone let the air out?"

"Zaid did. In the parking."

"And you watched?"

"I didn't do anything! I just stood there."

"Kunal walked home with his heavy bag. He was late for tuition."

"But Zaid did it, not me."

"If you had let the air out, how would you feel?"

"Bad. Really bad."

"And Kunal's tyre, is it less flat because you only watched?"

Farhan was quiet. "No."

"So?"

"So I'll help him pump it tomorrow." He paused. "And I'll tell Zaid it wasn't funny."

qa.q: Who let the air out of Kunal's tyre?
qa.a: Zaid did, in the parking.

qa.q: Why does Farhan keep saying "I didn't do anything"?
qa.a: He feels defensive and wants to believe he is innocent, because only watching feels much less guilty than doing it himself.

qa.q: How did Ammi help Farhan see the problem, and was it a good approach?
qa.a: She asked how he would feel if he had done it and whether the tyre was less flat, which let him see it himself instead of being lectured.

qa.q: What was it like for Kunal when his tyre was flat?
qa.a: Kunal had to walk home with a heavy bag and was late for tuition, so he was probably tired and upset.

grounding: A child feels innocent for watching a wrong rather than causing it, though the harm to his friend is the same.

passage:
Last month in class five, Nilesh copied my maths homework and handed it in first. I didn't tell him to copy it, and I didn't stop him either. When Sir asked who copied, both of us said nothing, and Sir gave the whole row extra work.

I kept thinking, it's not my fault. I didn't cheat. I only kept quiet.

But the girl next to me had done her own homework and still got extra work. She looked so upset, and I felt a heavy feeling in my stomach all day.

My name is Gautam. I think keeping quiet was a kind of doing something. Next time I'll say, "Nilesh, do your own," before it happens.

qa.q: What did Sir give the whole row?
qa.a: Sir gave the whole row extra work.

qa.q: Why did Gautam keep thinking "it's not my fault"?
qa.a: Gautam felt guilty, but only keeping quiet seemed milder than cheating, so the thought eased the uncomfortable feeling.

qa.q: What does Gautam plan to do next time, and why might it help?
qa.a: Gautam plans to tell Nilesh to do his own work before copying happens, which stops the harm instead of just staying out of it.

qa.q: How might the girl next to Gautam see what happened?
qa.a: She probably felt it was unfair and upset, since she had done her own homework and was still punished.

grounding: A child realises that staying silent about a classmate's copying felt innocent but still led to harm.

passage:
Class 4 teacher's note, last week before the winter break. Written by Vikas, class teacher.
Our class rabbit, Moti, got out of her cage during lunch and was found shivering behind the cupboard. Nobody meant any harm, but I asked what had happened.
Yusuf told me honestly that he had seen the cage door open before lunch. "But I didn't open it, Sir," he said, quite sure. "Someone else did. I just didn't close it." He felt much less bad than the boy who had left it open, though Moti got just as cold either way.
What I did next: I didn't scold. I asked Yusuf, "If you had opened it, would Moti be any colder?" He thought, and said no. Then I made both boys rabbit monitors for the week. Yusuf now checks the latch twice.

qa.q: Where was Moti found?
qa.a: Moti was found shivering behind the cupboard.

qa.q: Why did Yusuf feel less bad than the boy who left the door open?
qa.a: Yusuf felt that not closing the door was less guilty than opening it, so doing nothing felt innocent even though Moti got just as cold.

qa.q: What question did Vikas ask, and why was it useful?
qa.a: 'If you had opened it, would Moti be any colder?', which showed Yusuf that harm from not acting was the same as harm from acting.

qa.q: What was lunchtime like for Moti?
qa.a: Moti the rabbit got out, got cold and hid shivering behind the cupboard.

grounding: Shows, in a teacher's note, a child who feels less guilty for letting harm happen than for causing it.

passage:
Monsoon Tuesday.
Dear diary, today the neighbour's goat ate all of Mrs Pillai's tulsi and marigolds. Mrs Pillai cried a bit. Amma says it happened because the goat's rope was untied.
I saw it untied. At four, when I came home from school. I thought, not my goat, not my job, and went in to eat. Deepak saw it too, but he's six.
I told Amma, "I didn't untie it." She asked, "Did you see it?" I said yes. She didn't shout. She just said, "Mrs Pillai's plants are gone either way."
It's weird. Untying the goat feels like a real bad thing. Just walking past feels like nothing. But the tulsi is gone either way.
Tomorrow I'm helping Mrs Pillai replant. Amma is buying the saplings.
Kamal

qa.q: What did the goat eat?
qa.a: The goat ate all of Mrs Pillai's tulsi and marigolds.

qa.q: Why did walking past the untied goat feel like nothing to Kamal?
qa.a: Kamal felt calm and blameless, since someone else untied the rope, so walking past didn't feel like a bad thing.

qa.q: What is Kamal doing tomorrow, and why is it a good step?
qa.a: Helping Mrs Pillai replant, which takes responsibility for the harm that walking past allowed.

qa.q: How did the day feel for Mrs Pillai?
qa.a: Mrs Pillai was upset, even crying a bit, to find all her tulsi and marigolds eaten.

grounding: Shows a child who feels less guilty for letting harm happen than for causing it, until it is pointed out that the loss is the same.

passage:
In the dry month before the monsoon, the village in Bundelkhand counted every bucket. The courtyard water drum was filled only once a week.
On Thursday Ira saw the drum's tap dripping, then running. Her cousin had left it half open. Not me, Ira thought. I didn't touch it. She went off to play gilli-danda.
By evening the drum was half empty. Manjula Dadi stood beside it, silent.
"Did anyone see the tap?" she asked.
Ira's stomach twisted. "I saw it. But I didn't open it. Bittu did."
Dadi nodded slowly. "And the water ran out because of both of you. One opened it. One walked past."
Ira stared at the wet ground. Walking past had felt like nothing. But the drum didn't know the difference.
That night she walked to the well with Dadi and carried two buckets back without being asked.

qa.q: How often was the courtyard water drum filled?
qa.a: The drum was filled only once a week.

qa.q: Why did Ira walk past the running tap?
qa.a: Ira felt safe from blame because she didn't touch the tap, so not acting felt innocent and easy.

qa.q: What did Ira do that night, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Ira carried two buckets back from the well with Dadi, owning her part in the lost water.

qa.q: How might Manjula Dadi feel standing by the half-empty drum?
qa.a: Dadi likely felt worried and disappointed, knowing how precious water was in the dry month.

grounding: Shows a child who feels innocent for letting water run out because she didn't open the tap, though the harm was the same.

passage:
On the first snowy morning in Zaragoza, Mateo's class held a snowman contest in the playground. Hiroshi's snowman had pinecone eyes and a red scarf, the best one by far.
At break Mateo saw two older boys backing toward it, throwing snowballs and not looking. He could have shouted, "Watch out!" He opened his mouth, then closed it. They were big.
Crunch. The snowman's head rolled into the slush. Hiroshi stood very still, the scarf in his hand.
At home Mateo told his mum, "It's not my fault. I didn't touch it."
"And if you had bumped into it yourself?"
Mateo's face went hot. "That would be awful. I'd say sorry a hundred times." He looked at his boots. "But I didn't do anything."

qa.q: What did Hiroshi's snowman have?
qa.a: It had pinecone eyes and a red scarf.

qa.q: Why does Mateo feel it is not his fault?
qa.a: He didn't touch the snowman, so staying quiet feels innocent to him, though his hot face shows a flicker of guilt.

qa.q: What could Mateo do now to help?
qa.a: He could tell Hiroshi he is sorry he didn't shout a warning and offer to help rebuild the snowman, and next time call out even if the boys are big.

qa.q: What was it like for Hiroshi when the head rolled into the slush?
qa.a: Hiroshi stood very still with the scarf in his hand, probably shocked and sad that his best snowman was ruined while others watched.

grounding: Shows a child who feels less guilty for letting harm happen than he would for causing it himself.
